entry.content:
The escalation arrived as a refund threat. A customer had run acampaign, and thousands of people scanned its QR codes that dayexpecting to reach the sales team. One salesperson on the code hadalready hit his daily quota — the system showed him offline forassignment — and every new scan still connected to him. The rotation tothe next salesperson never fired. The campaign closed far below target,the customer demanded a refund, then churned: a six-figure annualcontract. The same mis-assignment had been producing quieter supporttickets for months. The logic was correct; the member list it computedfrom was not.

A live QR code is printed once and keeps working while the peoplebehind it change. The customer scans in WeChat, WeCom routes to whoever the codecurrently lists, and we maintain that list. At 30,000 tenants with 10 to20 staff on a QR code, most of them stayed idle until a campaign drovetraffic to them for days or weeks.

I owned this system — took it over as it stood. The tickets fell intotwo classes with one cause: staff shown offline still receiving scans,staff over quota still receiving scans.

The routing was never ours

WeCom owns the part that connects people. Tencent's enterprisemessenger matches each scan to a contact-wayconfiguration on its side and opens the chat with whoever thatconfig lists. Our platform never sees the scan that opens the chat. Soassignment, for us, meant one thing: maintaining that config. Decidingwhich staff IDs belong in it, and pushing every change through WeCom'sAPI.

Two stores had to agree. Our staff state — online, on duty, underquota, per tenant — lived in MongoDB. WeCom's config decidedwhere customers actually went. When the two disagreed, nothing raised anerror; production simply kept routing by the stale side, and scanslanded on someone we had marked offline an hour earlier. Repairing itwas not free either: the fix itself was a rate-limited API call with itsown failure modes.

The QR codes came in two families. Native codes handed memberselection to WeCom's random assignment, and our only job was whoappeared in the config. Sequenced and quota codes ran on our own landingpage, so we decided the order and the per-person volume as well. Theoffline and quota checks mattered most on these codes: a rotation thatnever happens is a list that never got updated.

Two years of features, sixwriters

Before I took over, feature work had put this state together piece bypiece:

  • State split across many collections. Online/offline flags (an adminendpoint, work-schedule timers), the per-staff-per-code ceiling records,the "already removed today" marker, and the counts that decided who wasfull — all in MongoDB, incremented by $inc on each scancallback. Four switches per code — offline check, add limit, dailylimit, round limit — plus a company-wide daily total decided how thosenumbers were applied.
  • Many paths wrote it. The scan callback, the admin offline endpoint,the quota counters, work-hours jobs, resignation handlers, org-changeevents. Each pushed its own update toward WeCom when it decided the listshould change: inline, with its own retry, at its own moment.
  • One slice already had a queue. Sequenced and quota codes used a RedisZSET with a two-level cursor, built by a teammate in 2021. Staffstate-change events went through Kafka to a consumer that adjustedthe set accordingly — full recompute on edits and shift changes, add areturning member, delete one who left or hit quota. Scans read the setthrough Lua.But every one of those paths went through the same consumer,asynchronously, and a full rebuild meant deleting and recreating thewhole key. Between "staff hit quota" and "set rebuilt without him",scans kept drawing the old membership.

Each path was sensible on its own; the bug was in none of them.The same state had many concurrent writers, and each writerpushed a list computed from a partial view.

Quiet days hid it: with little concurrent traffic, the writers rarelyinterleaved badly enough to lose a change. Campaign day removed thatsafety margin — scan volume and status changes peaked in the sameminutes, exactly when the gap between "state says stop" and "WeComconfig says go" was widest.

Both failure modes had been reaching support for months, as raretickets. Each was reproducible only under load, so each got chased as apossible logic bug and closed when no code defect turned up.

Three fixes that shouldhave worked

Once the defect was named — state and routing config drifting apart —three fixes suggested themselves. Each one fails on a structuralfact.

Check at scan time. Intercept the scan, read staffstate, route around anyone offline or over quota. For native codes thisis impossible in principle — the scan never touches our platform.Sequenced and quota codes do pass through our landing page, so the checkwas possible there — but it failed twice over. It put a database read onevery scan of the hottest path we had. Worse, it read the same state theconcurrent writers were updating, so the check itself could see a staleview and pass the person it was meant to skip.

Sweep and repair. A periodic job that walks every QRcode, compares our state against WeCom's config, and pushes a repairwhere they disagree. As a safety net this is the right shape, and itstayed on the list for later. As the primary fix it fails on arithmetic.WeComdocuments a ceiling of 10,000 calls a minute and 150,000 an hour perenterprise for a single API, and the 6M codes sit concentrated withheavy users: working through one heavy tenant's codes at that ceilingtakes tens of hours, in a window shared with the live pushes that keeparriving. This failure appears in minutes and has to be corrected inseconds; a sweep of tens of hours can only fix the slow kind ofdrift.

Better retries on every writer. Make every writepath idempotent, add exponential backoff, let each writer retry until itlands. This is the status quo with more machinery. A retry makes onewrite more likely to succeed; it says nothing about two writers pushinglists computed from different snapshots — last write wins, and thewinner's list is already stale. The defect was order, and retries do notorder anything.

All three patched where the symptom surfaced; the alternative was toremove the multiple writers.

One writer, recomputing

I put one Kafka queue between "state changed" and "WeCom configchanged". Every event that can alter a QR code's membership goes to onetopic, keyed by the QR code's own ID: an addition, a status flip, aschedule transition, a resignation, an org change, a config edit. Aconsumer group works through them. For each affected code it recomputesthe eligible members from current state, using the same four switcheseach old writer had checked on its own. It pushes that update to WeCom,and only then writes the result back to our store. WeCom is whererouting happens, so it gets the correct list first. And the store iswhat the dedupe check reads — the record of the last list successfullypushed — so it must only ever reflect completed pushes. Write the storefirst and the two writes can be split by a failed call: the record thenclaims a list WeCom never received, the redelivered event recomputes thesame list, the dedupe check matches it against the lying record, skipsthe call, and the divergence is permanent. The store is written onlyafter the push succeeds, so the dedupe record is never ahead of whatWeCom actually holds.

The state has to move before the event does. The counter that decideswho is full is a MongoDB document per staff member and code, incrementedby $inc. The consumer handling WeCom's customer-addedcallback increments it while it handles the addition, before itpublishes the refresh. By the time the refresh runs, the count iscurrent, and the event carries no counter value — the consumer reads thecount itself. Every other trigger follows the same rule: write the flagor the counter where the business event happens, then emit the refresh.Concurrency did not disappear — each handler still owns its own fact,and different facts never conflict. What the queue removed is the thingthe old writers raced on: concurrent composition of the same derivedlist. The queue carries a reason to recompute, not the state toapply.

Sequenced and quota codes still rotate on Redis, through the sameZSET and two-level cursor, but the two families now share one writer.For either family, the refresh consumer recomputes from the counts andflags as they stand and writes both routing targets — the config WeComreads and the set our landing page draws from — out of one computation,in one serial order. Before, each target had its own writer at its ownmoment — two writers for one code's membership, which was the race.

Serialization comes from the key. Events are keyed by the QR code'sID, and the consumer routes each key to a fixed goroutine, so one code'sevents apply one at a time while codes proceed in parallel. What needsordering is a single code's member list, and nothing else shares it. Theshared eventbus client we extended supplies that per-key mode, alongwith the retry path below.

The quota loop closes on the same queue, and it is where the loadcomes from. A scan callback increments a staff member's counter past theceiling. The handler marks the ceiling document with an idempotent"already removed today" flag, notifies the admin, looks up every codethat staff member sits on, and emits one membership event per QR code.Dozens of QR codes, sometimes more than a hundred. One removal becomesthat many WeCom pushes, and campaign day concentrates both the removalsand the QR codes.

What the constraints forced

Rate pressure and business freshness are two problems. The designseparates their cadence, not their budget — both lanes still draw on onerate window.

The lane a code runs in is a business decision: the tenant's tier,how fresh that code's membership has to be, an operator's switch. I keptthat decision a pure function evaluated per event — the code's creationand update age, a tenant whitelist — with no lane state stored anywhere.Every event starts on the fast topic; when the function says slow, theconsumer republishes it to the slow topic without a call. Producersnever judge lanes; the decision lives in one place, the serial consumer.A stateless call survives rebalances by construction, and a rule changetakes effect on the next event.

The cost of statelessness is a transition window. When policy flips acode from slow to fast, one event may still be queued on the slow topicwhile the next runs fast — briefly two in-flight workers for one code. Iaccepted that: both lanes run the same single-writer computation, theconsumer takes a per-code lock in Redis around each refresh, andwhichever push lands last was computed from the latest state. The nextbusiness event on that code recomputes from current state on the correctlane, so the divergence is transient by design — eventual consistency,bounded by how often the code's own traffic produces events.

The vendor's rate limit is handled optimistically, on the call path.Before calling WeCom, the handler makes two checks. The first is dedupe:compare the list just recomputed with the last list pushed for thatcode, and if they match there is nothing to send. That does not shrinkthe fan-out; ten QR codes with ten different lists are ten real pushes.It removes the no-ops — a retry, an edit that resolves to what isalready there.

The second check is the tenant's pre-limiter: a token bucket inRedis, spent through a Lua script so every instance counts against onewindow. With a token, push. Without one, the handler does not wait anddoes not hold the message open while the window refills. It acks asnot-done and requeues the event onto a retry topic with a delay — thepause is explicit, not a busy wait — after which it re-enters under thesame key, behind whatever that code's stream processed, through the sametwo checks. No second writer, and no consumer goroutine parkedmid-message.

Slow is a topic of its own, not a branch inside a handler: the slowlane enforces its interval by sleeping between a code's pushes — adeliberate down-throttle, not a message held open — and its workers areseparate from the fast lane's, so a sleeping slow worker parks only thatcode's slow stream and never delays the same code's fast events. Theinterval, seconds by policy, is the business decision, not the limiter.Both lanes draw on the same tenant's rate window — ordering is per code,the vendor's quota is not — so a code on slow competes with its tenant'sfast work for the vendor's limit. It draws fewer attempts from thatshared window.

A stateless lane call also means a code can linger on slow after aburst — extra delay, not divergence, on codes whose membership is notchanging. I took that staleness over maintaining per-code lanestate.

Failures do not hold the code's stream. A failed call is reported asnot-done and redelivered by the eventbus under the same key, instead ofbeing left unacknowledged while the consumer backs off. Holding theoffset would be the obvious choice and the wrong one even at codegranularity. A failing call in a retry storm pins its partition, and thecodes sharing that partition — a whole tenant's worth, under a busycampaign — wait behind it. Ack and redeliver keeps the blast radius atone code. WeCom's errors are specific enough to act on, too: a QR codedeleted on their side returns a distinct error, which the consumertreats as a cleanup trigger instead of a retry-forever case.

Requeueing gives up publish order; dropping gives up the messageafter a day. Neither matters: handlers recompute at processing time, soa late trigger reaches the same current truth, and a dropped event losesnothing that the next event would not recompute anyway. The design needsone writer per code. Arrival order was the part we could give up. Theresidual is a QR code no later event touches — staff went offline duringa multi-hour backlog, nothing followed, the stale list stays. CampaignQR codes are never idle that long, which is why the rule held inpractice: an assumption about traffic, not a guarantee about state.

What it cost, and what itbought

Migration ran as double-write through the second half of 2022 and cutover in early 2023. The new event chain went live while the oldsynchronous paths kept running; for weeks a diff job compared the memberlists the two paths pushed and alerted on any mismatch — it raised none.A config switch then retired the old paths. Tenant traffic did notnotice.

Freshness became bounded. Seconds on the fast lane, the slow lane'scadence, or the next redelivery after a throttled push, never theinstant of an inline write. After the new chain went live: p95 fromevent to WeCom's config under five seconds, measured from event publishto push completion in the metrics pipeline, and six consecutive monthswithout one ticket for either failure mode, against at least three amonth before.

WeCom's API became the explicit throughput ceiling. Under themulti-writer design nobody owned the rate limit; throttling showed up asscattered errors after the fact. One consumer made the ceiling visibleand manageable, with per-tenant rate limiting, redelivery on throttle,and robot alerts on throttle responses, and turned a recurring incidentsource into a scheduling parameter. The system held it: around 30,000tenants, around 6M live QR codes among heavy users, several hundredscans per second in short campaign spikes, peak-day volume under amillion.

One dependency more than before. Kafka availability now gatesmembership updates. The failure mode errs toward safety: if the queuestalls, updates are delayed rather than misapplied, and scans runagainst the last consistent list. The real cost is operational. A secondsystem to monitor, plus poison messagesand lag, a class of bug MongoDB-only code never had.

The churned account came back. After running on the refactored systemfor a while, they re-subscribed. A customer who has lost technical trustdoes not return for a discount.

These are production numbers, not a load test, and the complaintrecord is the proof. I leave the incident account's campaign lossunquantified on purpose: it is the customer's data, not ours to publish.The churn and the re-subscription carry that part of the argument.

What I would keep, andwhat I left open

I would keep the central decision: one serialized queue, keyed by theQR code, applying to WeCom first and our store second.

The production surprise was that serialization was the easy part;living with WeCom's rate limits was the long tail. If I designed itagain, I would budget the dependency's shape too: the rate window andthe drain rate should come from the fan-out arithmetic — how many liveQR codes a member sits on — not the event rate, which understates callsby that factor. Coalescing is half-built: a Redis marker drops a newrefresh event while one for the same code is still queued; the missinghalf is merging events at push time, since the push replaces the wholelist.

On Pulsar I would trycollapsing the lanes into subscription semantics: one topic with aKey_Shared subscription keyed by the QR code ID. The broker routes eachkey to a single consumer, so the fast/slow split, the separate workersets, the per-code lock, and the hand-rolled retry topic all disappear —a demotion or a throttle becomes a negative ack with a redelivery delay,the same ack-as-not-done pattern we had built by hand on Kafka. Aredelivered message can come back out of order, which is the arrivalorder the design had already given up.

Reconciliation is the part I never closed. The rejected sweep had theneed right; its shape was the problem. The queue guarantees a freshread, not a correct outcome — a bug in the recompute gets applied justas consistently. But 6M QR codes at the documented rate limits is tensof hours of work to protect a handful of suspects. The backstop shouldbe a dirty set — codes whose events were dropped, whose pushes failedpermanently, or whose recomputes errored — swept at low frequency. Wehad no such layer; the evidence was customer complaints, weaker than asystem this size should run on.

One boundary is permanent: assignment lives in WeCom's config, andnothing inside our platform makes that system synchronous with us — thedesign only keeps the delay across it bounded and visible.

entry.content:
During load testing, room ticks began overrunning their 50 ms budgetas simulated clients reached target density. Normal ticks took 10–20 ms;spikes took 100–300 ms, leaving clients two to six ticks behind. We hadbuilt the room service for a QQ-licensed casual pet game. It wasdesigned for tens of millions of users; actual peak concurrency reachedroughly 200,000 players.

I led the architecture selection and ECS implementation. Profilingshowed how much CPU time component lookups consumed.

Designing for 10,000players per instance

Tencent's publishing team planned to roll out access in stages. Theservice needed to absorb each traffic increase by adding instances. Loadtests used a fleet of slightly lower-spec instances running bots throughthe real client protocol: entering rooms, moving, and collecting. Thetarget was 10,000 real players per server instance: about 667 rooms withfifteen players each, updated at 20 Hz.

Late room-state updates led us to investigate the room's serialupdate cycle.

Outside rooms, another service handled idle collection throughrequest-response calls. Inside rooms, players shared a grid of up to200×200 cells for movement, exploration, combat, and collection.Clicking a destination triggered server-side pathfinding. Playermovement step size was defined separately from the simulation tick. Aroom held about fifteen real players, 30+ combat NPCs, and a varyingnumber of bot players, with a room capacity of 30–100, depending on roomclass. The room service updated shared state on each tick, with threeconstraints:

  • Responsive movement. Delayed server updates were visible toplayers.
  • A bounded update cycle per room. Each room updated every 50 ms (20Hz), and all work for that tick had to finish within the interval.
  • Bounded broadcast fanout. Room population and visibility limits hadto cap the audience for each update.

Choosing theroom boundary and its execution model

I made two choices: which state each execution unit would own, andhow it would run the simulation. Actor-styleownership determined who held mutable state and how work reached it.ECSdetermined how components were stored and systems iterated overthem.

Keeping shared statewithin one room

Giving each player its own actor would separate ownership of playerstate, but interactions involving multiple players and shared room statewould require coordination between actors. For example, if two playersclaimed the same collection cell within one tick, an actorimplementation could resolve the conflict by giving a room actorauthority over the cell and routing both claims to it. The cost isforwarding requests, returning results, and defining when the playeractors apply those results. Visibility queries, movement collisions, andPvP interactions raise the same ownership question. I kept theinteracting state under one room owner, so these operations couldcomplete within one simulation pass.

An actor-based design can also batch inputs and resolve them in astable order; Proto.Actorprovides a Go implementation of actor messaging. When player state issplit across actors, the design must also define tick boundaries andcoordinate the state used in each tick.

A single global simulation loop would couple unrelated rooms: a slowroom would delay the others, and the serial loop could not use multipleprocessors.

Choosing ECS for the roominterior

The closest alternative was a room-level actor: one goroutine andmailbox per room, with entities stored as objects and events handled bymethods. It provided the same ownership boundary as the shipped design.In the candidate design, handlers processed messages in arrival orderand dispatched each event separately. My tick-based design batched theframe's inputs and let systems query components directly for operationssuch as finding the players within an area of interest (AOI).

I chose ECS to support frequent gameplay changes inside existingrooms. Components held buff effects and expiration times; systemsapplied the effects in tick order. Items could reuse the same componentsand systems. Adding mechanics this way reduced branching in playerobjects and message handlers.

I could order buff application, movement, damage calculation, andexpiration explicitly, with no concurrent writes inside the room. Fixedinputs and simulation time made interactions between mechanics easier toreproduce in tests.

The speed-item example below uses an array-based ECS.EntityID indexes the component arrays, and masks recordwhich components are present on each entity. Room.Tick runsitem application, buff expiration, and movement serially. Adding orremoving a component changes membership while retaining itspre-allocated slot.

Each tick simulates the 50 ms interval beginning atnowMS. Buffs are active on[appliedAt, expiresAt), so a buff expiring at 100 ms doesnot affect movement over [100, 150). Durations align withticks, and each player can have one speed buff. Positions usethousandths of a cell; distance depends on speed and elapsed time.

Save as main.go and run go run main.go:

Output (positions in thousandths of a cell):

The position-only entity stays still, and the control player keepsits base speed. The buffed player returns to base speed at theexpiration boundary.

A room-level actor could implement the same gameplay and tests,including ECS internally. In the candidate's event-handler design,interactions between effects would require ordering rules acrosshandlers. I chose component composition and an explicit system sequenceto keep those rules together as gameplay grew.

In the shipped service, one goroutine owned each room's mutablestate, and Go'sruntime scheduled room goroutines across the available processors.Systems ran serially within that goroutine, accessing components for therelevant entities on every tick.

Cross-room state lived on a separate tier with its own consistencyrules, so features spanning rooms required additional coordination.

A slow entity could delay its room's tick while unrelated roomscontinued, provided the process and scheduler stayed healthy. Extracores could run other rooms, but could not shorten that room's serialtick. A room that exceeded its deadline needed less work per tick,further optimization, or a lower population cap.

Roomscheduling, serial ticks, and state management

Each instance pooled rooms, pre-allocating them to keep allocationoff the hot path and recycling them as demand fell. Players joined roomclasses matching their level and intent, keeping new players amongpeers. A central scheduler tracked instance load and placed each newroom on the least-loaded instance.

I initially stored components in entity-keyed maps to supportchanging entity counts without reserving full-capacity arrays for everyroom. Rooms with fewer entities could allocate storage as needed, thoughmaps carried their own bucket and key overhead. Each system looked upcomponents while iterating its entities. Player input arrived throughthe connection layer; each tick consumed the inputs accumulated sincethe previous update.

State changes were sent only to players whose area of interestincluded the affected location. PvP interaction used the same visibilityboundary. AOI filtering and room population caps bounded broadcastfanout.

Persistence ran outside the tick. Room snapshots were takenasynchronously and flushed periodically to MongoDB. A restart restoredeach room from its last persisted snapshot, potentially losingsubsequent updates. That was acceptable for this casual game. Snapshotflush lag and the recovery loss window were not measured; I would addmetrics for both.

Map lookups exhausted thetick budget

pprofshowed map operations consuming 60–85% of the profiled CPU time. Thesefigures reflect the load-test results I confirmed at the time; they arenot quoted from retained profiles. The hot frame wasaeshash, Go's AES-NI-based hash implementation. The Go 1.13runtime routed maplookups through its hashingfunctions to AESENC-basedcode.

Across all systems and rooms, component lookups required roughly 13million hash computations per second per instance, before buckettraversal and key comparison. Map insertions and growth addedallocations. GC ran about once a second during the test. Entity IDscould directly index component arrays; the maps added a hash lookup toeach access.

I kept the room boundary and serial system order, and replacedcomponent maps with pre-allocated fixed-capacity arrays indexed byentity ID. Storage was reused across room lifecycles. Sequentialcomponent traversal also favored cache locality, though cache misseswere not measured separately.

Pre-allocated arrays reserved space up to each room's entity cap evenwhen occupancy was low. Room reuse saved allocation work but retainedthat storage. Growing arrays with occupancy or grouping entities bycomponent set could reduce unused slots, but would addstorage-management work. I accepted the reserved space to keep lookupsdirect and reuse storage.

After the change, p99 tick elapsed time, measured withtime.Since, fell below 50 ms, and instance CPU utilizationsettled near 70%. Profiles showed less hot-path allocation churn, but Ido not have before-and-after measurements of GC pause frequency.

Broadcast fanout was not the bottleneck in this test. The tickoverruns were resolved before production.

Production results andcapacity

At 10,000 players per instance and fifteen players per room, eachinstance ran about 667 rooms at 20 Hz. A typical room contained roughly60–80 entities: players, combat NPCs, bots, and collection objects. Atthat density, the 8-vCPU instance averaged 70% CPU utilization duringthe same load-test window. Dividing its CPU consumption by the number ofroom ticks gives about 0.42 ms per room tick:

This average includes connection handling, serialization, GC, andother instance work.

Room goroutines waited between updates, allowing hundreds of rooms toshare the 8 vCPUs. We added instances as room density approached theper-instance limit.

The memory model was:

Estimated per-room memory was a few hundred KiB at fifteen players.At ~667 rooms per instance, that amounted to a few hundred MiB. The 16GiB instances also provided capacity for the Go process, playerconnections, queues, snapshots, caches, runtime metadata, and headroom.The fleet used the same instance configuration throughout: 8 vCPU / 16GiB on TencentCloud.

Concurrency outside activity peaks was in the tens of thousands. Asingle instance carried over 10,000 concurrent players. At activitypeaks, the fleet served roughly 200,000 concurrent players across 20+instances, with over one million DAU.

The talk Overwatch GameplayArchitecture and Netcode gave me many of the ideas behind thisdesign, especially separating component state from system behavior andorganizing data for sequential access.
